title: Design a CDN
scopeHtml: Scope: edge caches, routing via DNS and anycast, cache hierarchy, invalidation, TLS, origin shielding.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A CDN (content delivery network) keeps copies of content on servers near users, so pages, images and videos load fast and the origin server is not overwhelmed. Cloudflare, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront, Fastly and Netflix's Open Connect are CDNs. Distance costs time: light in fibre covers about 200 km per ms, so Mumbai to Virginia is ~200 ms round trip, while Mumbai to a Mumbai edge is ~5 ms.

Functional

  • Serve static content (images, JS, CSS, video segments) from the edge.
  • On a miss, fetch from the customer's origin, cache, and serve.
  • Customers can purge/invalidate content and set cache rules (TTL).
  • HTTPS for customer domains; support for range requests (video).

Non-functional

  • Low latency: first byte under 50 ms for hits.
  • Very high availability (99.99%+) and DDoS resilience.
  • Huge bandwidth: terabits per second globally.
  • High cache hit ratio (95%+) to protect origins.
  • Efficient: less origin egress cost.

Decision gravity. Pull CDN (edge fetches from origin on demand) versus push CDN (customer uploads content to edge in advance). Pull is simpler and the default for the web; push suits large, predictable media (Netflix pre-positions popular titles overnight). Reversible per content type.

Everyday analogy. Local warehouses: instead of shipping every parcel from one factory abroad, popular items sit in a warehouse in your city.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying a CDN is only for images; it also does TLS, DDoS protection, API acceleration.
  • Forgetting dynamic/personalised content cannot be cached the same way.
  • Ignoring invalidation.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Two audiences: end users (plain HTTP) and customers (control plane).

Data plane (user)

GET /static/app.js HTTP/2
Host: assets.customer.com

HTTP/2 200
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
ETag: "9f2c1a"
Age: 1432
X-Cache: HIT from edge-bom-12
Content-Encoding: br

Conditional revalidation: If-None-Match: "9f2c1a" gives 304 Not Modified. Video: Range: bytes=0-1048575 gives 206 Partial Content.

Control plane (customer)

POST /v1/distributions
{ "domain": "assets.customer.com",
  "origin": { "host": "origin.customer.com", "protocol": "https" },
  "defaultTtlSeconds": 86400,
  "rules": [ { "path": "/api/*", "cache": false },
             { "path": "/img/*", "ttlSeconds": 604800 } ] }
201 { "id": "dist_123", "cname": "dist123.cdn.example.net" }

POST /v1/distributions/dist_123/invalidations
{ "paths": ["/img/logo.png", "/css/*"] }
202 { "invalidationId": "inv_9", "status": "in_progress" }

GET  /v1/distributions/dist_123/analytics?from=...&to=...
200 { "hitRatio": 0.96, "bytesServed": 8200000000000 }

Customer points their DNS: assets.customer.com CNAME dist123.cdn.example.net.

Industry example. CloudFront's invalidation API accepts path patterns and typically takes seconds to a few minutes to complete globally; Fastly advertises purge in about 150 ms using surrogate keys.

Everyday analogy. The customer gives the warehouse a list of products, how long they stay fresh, and a way to recall a product.

Common interview traps.

  • Using invalidation as the main update mechanism instead of versioned filenames.
  • No Cache-Control strategy.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume a CDN serving 10 billion requests/day, average object 100 KB, with video excluded; plus video streaming.

Quantity Calculation Result
Requests/s 10B / 86,400 ~116k/s average, ~350k/s peak
Egress 116k x 100 KB ~11.6 GB/s = 93 Gbps average, ~280 Gbps peak
Video example 10M concurrent viewers x 4 Mbps 40 Tbps
Edge server capacity 1 server with 2 x 100 Gbps NICs, SSD cache ~100 Gbps effective
Servers for 280 Gbps 280 / 100 3 (plus redundancy), but spread across ~50 locations
Cache storage per edge Hot set of the region's content 20 to 100 TB SSD
Origin offload at 96% hit 350k/s x 4% 14k/s to origins instead of 350k/s

Netflix serves a large share of peak US evening traffic from Open Connect appliances (storage servers placed inside ISPs). The numbers are why CDNs exist: origin bandwidth and cost would be impossible otherwise.

Everyday analogy. Counting how many local warehouses you need from how many parcels per second each region orders.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing bits and bytes (Gbps vs GB/s: multiply by 8).
  • Not separating small-object request-rate limits from large-object bandwidth limits.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • PoPs (points of presence): data centres or racks in many cities and ISPs, each with many edge servers behind local load balancing.
  • Request routing: send the user to a nearby, healthy, non-overloaded PoP using DNS-based steering, or anycast IP routing (same IP advertised from many PoPs; BGP picks the nearest).
  • Edge cache: memory (hot) + SSD (warm) store of objects, keyed by URL + selected headers.
  • Mid-tier / regional cache and origin shield: extra layers that collapse many edge misses into a single origin fetch.
  • Control plane: config, certificates, purge propagation, analytics, health monitoring.
  • Origin: customer servers or object storage (S3).

Decision gravity. Anycast versus DNS steering: anycast is simple, resilient to PoP failure (BGP withdraws the route) and absorbs DDoS across many PoPs, but gives less control over load. DNS steering gives fine control with TTL-limited reaction time and relies on resolver location accuracy. Large CDNs use both. Changing the routing layer is operationally risky but possible in stages.

Industry examples. Cloudflare is anycast-first; Akamai pioneered DNS mapping with ~300k+ servers inside ISPs; Netflix steers clients via its control plane (client asks the Netflix API which Open Connect box to use) rather than plain DNS.

Everyday analogy. A chain of shops: neighbourhood store, then city depot, then central warehouse, then the factory.

Common interview traps.

  • A flat design where every edge talks straight to the origin (10,000 simultaneous misses on a new video).
  • Forgetting health checks that remove a failing PoP from routing.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Request routing: DNS vs anycast

  • DNS steering: the CDN's authoritative DNS looks at the resolver's IP (or the EDNS Client Subnet), picks the best PoP using latency, load and health, and returns its IP with a short TTL (30 to 60 s). Weakness: users on a far-away public resolver (8.8.8.8) can be mis-located; ECS helps.
  • Anycast: the same IP is announced via BGP from every PoP; routers send packets to the topologically nearest one. Failure handling is automatic (withdraw the route). Weakness: BGP "nearest" is not always lowest latency, and long-lived TCP connections can break if routing shifts (mitigated with consistent hashing at the PoP and QUIC connection IDs).

Cache hierarchy and request collapsing

On an edge miss, ask the regional tier; on a miss there, ask the origin shield, which is the only place that calls the origin. Benefits: origin sees a tiny, predictable load.

Request collapsing (coalescing): if 5,000 users request an uncached object in the same second, the edge sends one origin request and holds the others until it returns. Prevents a thundering herd after a cache purge or a viral release.

Worked example. A new 5 MB image goes viral: 200 PoPs x 1 miss each = 200 requests to the shield, which makes 1 origin request. Without a shield: 200 origin requests; without collapsing: thousands.

Cache keys, TTLs and freshness

  • Cache key = scheme + host + path + normalised query + selected headers (for example Accept-Encoding). Strip tracking parameters (utm_*) to avoid fragmenting the cache. Use Vary carefully: Vary: User-Agent can explode the number of variants.
  • Freshness from Cache-Control: max-age, s-maxage (CDN only), Expires. After expiry the edge revalidates with If-None-Match (cheap 304).
  • stale-while-revalidate / stale-if-error: serve stale content instantly while fetching a fresh copy, or when the origin is down. A big availability win.
  • Eviction: LRU or smarter (LFU/TinyLFU, SLRU) on SSD; a one-hit-wonder filter (a Bloom filter admits an object to disk only on its second request) saves a lot of disk writes since a large share of objects are requested once.
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400

Invalidation and versioning

Phil Karlton's joke: only two hard things in CS are cache invalidation and naming. Options:

  1. Versioned URLs (best): app.3f9c2a.js with max-age=31536000, immutable. A new deploy gets a new name; no purge needed.
  2. Purge by URL/pattern: control plane pushes a purge message to all PoPs (pub/sub tree); takes seconds to minutes.
  3. Surrogate keys / cache tags: tag objects (product-42) and purge by tag (Fastly, Cloudflare).
  4. Short TTLs with revalidation for content that must be fresh.

Decision gravity. Choosing versioned filenames shifts complexity to the build system but removes a whole class of stale-content bugs. Relying on purge is reversible but operationally fragile.

Large files and video

Video is split into 2 to 10 s segments (HLS/DASH), each a separate small cacheable object; players adapt bitrate. Edge supports Range requests, and cache slices (for example 1 MB chunks) so a partial request does not require fetching the whole file. Netflix pre-fills popular titles to appliances overnight (push) based on predicted popularity and serves from SSD/NVMe at ~100+ Gbps per box.

TLS and security

  • Terminate TLS at the edge (TLS 1.3, session resumption, OCSP stapling), cutting handshake latency from far to near; edge-to-origin uses a persistent, reused connection pool.
  • Certificates are issued automatically (ACME/Let's Encrypt or customer-provided), distributed by the control plane; SNI picks the right one.
  • DDoS: absorb at the edge using anycast capacity, rate limiting, WAF and bot checks. Cloudflare has mitigated attacks of several Tbps.
  • Signed URLs/cookies for private content (expiring tokens), origin access restrictions (only CDN IPs allowed).

Dynamic content and failure handling

Even uncacheable API traffic benefits: TLS termination near the user, TCP/QUIC optimisation, and an optimised backbone to the origin (Cloudflare Argo, Akamai SureRoute). Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) runs code at the edge.

Failures: PoP outage (route withdrawn, traffic moves to the next PoP, which then sees a cold cache and a surge of origin misses: mitigate with shield and stale-if-error); origin outage (serve stale); poisoned cache (a bad response cached widely: be careful which status codes are cacheable, cache 5xx for at most a few seconds).

Production incident pattern. Symptom: sudden origin CPU/bandwidth spike and slow pages. Metric: edge hit ratio drops. Causes: a deploy that changed cache keys, a mass purge, or cookies added to previously cacheable requests. Fix: check Vary, Set-Cookie and query-string handling; enable request collapsing and stale-while-revalidate.

Everyday analogy. The origin shield is a single manager who orders from the factory on behalf of all the city stores, so the factory never gets 200 identical orders at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Caching responses with Set-Cookie or per-user data and leaking one user's page to another.
  • Ignoring cache-key fragmentation from query strings.
  • Purging everything during a deploy and hammering the origin.
  • No stale-if-error plan.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Distinguish pull vs push, static vs dynamic, and what is cacheable.
  • Routing: DNS and anycast with trade-offs.
  • Multi-tier caching, origin shield and request collapsing; the numbers showing origin offload.
  • Cache semantics: keys, TTLs, Vary, revalidation, stale directives, eviction.
  • Invalidation strategies, favouring versioned URLs.
  • Security: TLS termination, DDoS, signed URLs, private content.
  • Seniors discuss video delivery (segments, ABR, pre-positioning), cost (egress and peering), multi-CDN failover, observability (hit ratio, TTFB, 5xx per PoP) and ISP-embedded caches.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating the CDN as a black box without explaining how a request finds the nearest edge.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A CDN caches content at edge PoPs near users; pull on miss is the default, push for predictable heavy media.
  • Route users with anycast and/or DNS steering with health and load awareness.
  • Use tiers: edge, regional, origin shield; collapse concurrent misses so the origin sees a trickle.
  • Control freshness via cache keys, Cache-Control, revalidation and stale-while-revalidate/if-error; evict with LRU/LFU and admit selectively.
  • Prefer versioned URLs over purges; use surrogate keys when you must purge.
  • Terminate TLS and absorb DDoS at the edge; protect private content with signed URLs.
  • Edge hit ratio is the core health metric: 96% means the origin sees 1/25 of the traffic.

questions.subtopic: What a CDN does, pull vs push
questions.promptHtml: What does a CDN actually do for a website, and what is the difference between a pull CDN and a push CDN?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you can explain the core idea without buzzwords, and that you know a CDN is about latency and origin protection, not only images.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I'd say a CDN keeps copies of content on servers close to users, so a request is answered from a nearby edge instead of travelling to the origin. That cuts latency (Mumbai to Virginia is about 200 ms round trip, Mumbai to a Mumbai edge about 5 ms) and keeps most traffic off the origin. In a pull CDN the edge fetches from the origin on the first miss and caches it. In a push CDN the customer uploads content to the edge ahead of time. Pull is the web default; push suits large, predictable media.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pull:  User -> Edge (miss) -> Origin -> Edge stores copy -> User
       next user -> Edge (hit) -> User
Push:  Customer -> uploads to Edge/storage in advance -> User always hits
  • Pull is lazy: no work for content nobody asks for, and no coordination with the customer. The cost is that the first user per edge pays a miss, and a cold cache after a purge sends a burst to the origin.
  • Push gives zero first-request penalty, but you must decide what to push, where, and when to delete. It fits a movie catalogue where you can predict popularity (Netflix fills appliances overnight).
  • A CDN also terminates TLS near the user, absorbs DDoS using the capacity of many PoPs, and can accelerate uncacheable API calls over a better backbone.
  • The metric that matters is the cache hit ratio. At 96% the origin sees 1/25 of the traffic.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "a CDN is for images and static files only". Dynamic traffic also benefits from TLS termination and connection reuse.
  • Thinking pull means "slow". Only the first request per edge is slow.
  • Forgetting that push needs a deletion and update story.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which content can not be cached the same way? -> Per-user or personalised responses, unless the cache key includes the user or you cache only the shared fragment.
  2. Why does the customer set a CNAME? -> So the customer's domain resolves into the CDN's DNS, which can steer each user to a nearby PoP.
  3. How would you mix pull and push? -> Pull for the long tail, push (pre-position) for a new release you know will be hot, per content type.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer stops at "it caches static files near users". The senior answer adds hit ratio and origin offload math, the cost of a cold edge, and the decision gravity: pull versus push is reversible per content type.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that launch a big release on a pull CDN with a cold cache often see the origin spike for the first minutes; pre-warming or a shield avoids it.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says only: "Design a CDN for our company." The company has a marketing site (mostly static), a logged-in web app, a public JSON API and a growing video library. No other numbers are given.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Jumps straight to "put Redis caches in many regions". It never asks what is cacheable, what the scale is, or who operates the CDN (build versus buy), so the design may solve the wrong problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Are we building a CDN product for customers, or using one for our own sites? That changes everything: a control plane with customer APIs versus a CloudFront config. (b) What traffic split is static, API, video, and how much of it is per-user? That decides the cacheable share. (c) Scale: requests/s, Gbps and peak (a launch day)? (d) Where are users, and what first-byte target (say under 50 ms for hits)? (e) How fast must content update: seconds, minutes, deploy-time only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd state assumptions out loud so the interviewer can correct me: 10 billion requests/day, average 100 KB object, video separate, pull model.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Marketing site plus images plus JS/CSS gives the highest hit ratio and the least risk. Video is the biggest bandwidth. The API is mostly uncacheable but still gains from TLS termination. The logged-in app needs care so private data is never shared.
  4. How I'd verify each: Ask for a week of access logs and compute per-path share of bytes, requests and Set-Cookie/Authorization presence. That gives a real cacheable-bytes estimate instead of a guess.
  5. Root cause: The design depends on the cacheable fraction, so that is the first number to pin down.
  6. Fix: Propose a plan: pull CDN, versioned filenames for assets, short TTL plus revalidation for HTML, no-cache rules for /api/* and anything with cookies, HLS segments cached long, edge plus shield tiers, purge by tag.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards for hit ratio, TTFB, 5xx per PoP, and origin offload, agreed upfront as success criteria.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not build my own global PoP network for one company. Buying (CloudFront, Fastly, Cloudflare, Akamai) is reversible and cheaper until traffic is huge; building is a one-way door in cost and staffing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the interviewer says "we are building the CDN as a product"? -> Then add a control plane (distributions, rules, certificates, purge, analytics), multi-tenancy isolation and billing by bytes.
  • What if 80% of traffic carries a session cookie? -> Strip cookies from static paths at the edge, put per-user content behind separate paths or use edge compute, and measure the cache hit ratio again.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team put a CDN in front of the whole domain with default rules. The home page for logged-in users was cached for a few minutes and showed one user's name to another. The fix was explicit allow-listing of cacheable paths, not the other way around.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Starts drawing boxes with no questions.
  • Hire: Asks scale, cacheability and build-versus-buy, and states assumptions.
  • Strong hire: Proposes pulling real access logs to size the cacheable share, separates static, video and API, and names the decision gravity.

questions.subtopic: Cache keys, Vary, TTL and revalidation
questions.promptHtml: How does a CDN decide two requests are "the same" object, and how does it decide how long to keep it? Where does this go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cache key mistakes are the most common reason a CDN has a poor hit ratio or serves wrong content. It shows whether you understand the HTTP caching contract.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The cache key is scheme plus host plus path plus a normalised query plus the headers I choose, for example Accept-Encoding. Freshness comes from Cache-Control: max-age for everyone, s-maxage for shared caches such as the CDN. After expiry the edge revalidates with If-None-Match and usually gets a cheap 304. It goes wrong when the key is too wide (tracking parameters, Vary: User-Agent) so the cache fragments, or too narrow so one user's variant is served to another.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GET /img/a.png?utm_source=x   -> key A
GET /img/a.png?utm_source=y   -> key B   (same bytes, two copies, two misses)
  • Normalise: sort the query string, drop utm_* and other tracking parameters, lowercase the host.
  • Vary tells caches which request headers change the response. Vary: Accept-Encoding gives two or three variants (br, gzip, identity). Vary: User-Agent gives thousands.
  • Example header: Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400. Browsers keep it 60 s, the CDN 1 h. stale-while-revalidate serves the old copy while fetching; stale-if-error serves stale if the origin is down.
  • Eviction is LRU or an LFU variant (TinyLFU/SLRU). A one-hit-wonder filter (admit to disk only on the second request) saves SSD writes, since a large share of objects are requested once.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving query strings in the key, so ?v=1&utm=... variants never hit.
  • Vary: Cookie on a public page, which makes almost every request a miss.
  • Caching a response that has Set-Cookie or per-user data.
  • Using a long TTL without versioned filenames, then needing a purge for every change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why s-maxage separately from max-age? -> You can keep a long CDN TTL while the browser rechecks often, and purge the CDN when needed.
  2. What does a 304 save? -> The body transfer; the edge refreshes its freshness timer with a tiny response.
  3. How would you protect the origin when many keys expire at the same instant? -> Request collapsing at the edge and shield, plus stale-while-revalidate, plus TTL jitter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "set a TTL". The senior answer designs the key deliberately, names the stale directives, and knows Vary can multiply the variants.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deploy that added a cache-busting query parameter to every link dropped a site's hit ratio from 95% to 40% in minutes and tripled origin load.

questions.contextHtml:
A CDN-fronted shop normally shows a 96% edge hit ratio. After a 14:05 release the dashboard shows:

time    hit_ratio  origin_rps  origin_cpu  p99_ttfb
14:00   0.96       14k         22%         48 ms
14:10   0.31       240k        91%         1,900 ms

The release changed the front-end bundle, added a tracking cookie via Set-Cookie: sid=... on every response, and the team also upgraded the origin framework. The CDN vendor status page is green.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, and what do you suspect?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Purge and warm the cache" (a purge makes it worse) or blaming the CDN vendor without looking at a single response header.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly changed at 14:05 (headers, cookies, URLs, query parameters)? Is it all paths or some? Did the miss reason change (X-Cache: MISS versus BYPASS)? Is the CDN configured to bypass cache when Set-Cookie is present?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the release or flip the flag that adds the cookie. Raise the origin autoscaling floor. Turn on stale-while-revalidate/stale-if-error and keep serving old objects. Do NOT purge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Set-Cookie on static responses makes the CDN treat them as uncacheable. (b) New query parameter or Vary changed the cache key. (c) The framework upgrade changed Cache-Control defaults (for example private or no-store). (d) A mass purge or TTL change. The vendor outage is last given the green status.
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -sI https://shop.com/static/app.js twice and compare Cache-Control, Vary, Set-Cookie, Age, X-Cache. Diff headers against a pre-release response. Group edge logs by cache status and reason.
  5. Root cause: Typically the cookie on previously cacheable responses; the edge honours "do not cache responses that set cookies" and every request goes to the origin.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove the cookie from static and image paths or have the CDN ignore it for those paths. Long-term: separate a cookie-free static domain, cache rules in code review, a header snapshot test in CI.
  7. Prevention: Alert on hit ratio dropping more than 10 points in 5 minutes. A synthetic check that asserts Cache-Control and absence of Set-Cookie on key assets.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not purge or add servers blindly: the origin is overloaded because misses spiked, and a purge multiplies them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if hit ratio recovers but origin load stays high? -> Check request collapsing and the shield; the cache key may still be fragmented.
  • What if the rollback is blocked? -> Edge rule to strip Set-Cookie and normalise the cache key for /static/*.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An analytics snippet started setting a cookie from the server on every asset. Hit ratio fell from 94% to 18% before anyone checked a header. The fix was one edge rule and a CI header test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Purges or blames the vendor.
  • Hire: Inspects headers, finds cookie/key change, rolls back.
  • Strong hire: Mitigates origin first, avoids purging, adds a CI header assertion and an alert.

questions.contextHtml: A streaming customer expects 10M concurrent viewers for a live match at an average of 4 Mbps, with 4 s segments in 5 renditions. Your edge server has 2 x 100 Gbps NICs and about 100 Gbps effective throughput. You run roughly 50 PoPs. The finance lead asks how many edge servers are needed and how much traffic hits the origin.
questions.promptHtml: Do the math and say what you would verify.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Mixes Gbps and GB/s, ignores the target utilisation and redundancy, and says "origin handles it, it is just 10M users".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the stream live or VOD (live means few unique objects)? Is the 4 Mbps average or the top rung? What is the peak versus average? Is the traffic concentrated in a few countries?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (planning). I would book capacity ahead and test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The bandwidth is the binding constraint, not requests per second, because segments are about 2 MB.
  4. How I'd verify each: Egress = 10M x 4 Mbps = 40 Tbps = 5 TB/s. At 100 Gbps per server that is 400 servers at 100% utilisation. I would plan at 60-70% utilisation, so about 600 servers, plus N+1 per PoP, spread across 50 PoPs: roughly 12 per PoP, weighted by where the audience is. Segment rate: 4 Mbps x 4 s = 16 Mbit = 2 MB per segment, so 10M viewers / 4 s = 2.5M segment requests/s. For the origin: a live event has only about 5 renditions x 1 new segment per 4 s = 1.25 unique objects/s. With edge, regional and shield collapsing, origin sees a few requests/s per rendition, not 2.5M.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The result: bandwidth-bound edge, tiny origin load for live, but a VOD or catch-up long tail would be very different.
  6. Fix: Pre-warm the shield, make sure request collapsing is on, cap manifest TTL at 2-6 s, and ask ISPs about embedded caches for the largest audiences.
  7. Prevention: Load-test a few PoPs with a synthetic player at the target rate, and watch per-PoP NIC saturation, hit ratio and TTFB in the event.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not size for average load; the kickoff moment is a spike. I would not trust the vendor's headline capacity without a test.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the audience is 60% in one country? -> Weight PoPs there and use multi-CDN so one provider's saturation does not stop the event.
  • What if viewers mostly pick the 1080p rung? -> Bitrate average rises, so the 40 Tbps goes up; use player and per-title ladder tuning.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sized only by request rate; on match day one PoP's uplinks saturated while the rest idled. Steering by load, not only by distance, fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Gets bits and bytes wrong, ignores headroom.
  • Hire: 40 Tbps, server count with headroom, origin offload.
  • Strong hire: Separates live from VOD uniqueness, adds multi-CDN and ISP caches, and plans a load test.

questions.contextHtml:
At 20:12 a power event takes the Mumbai PoP offline. Anycast withdraws the route and traffic moves to Chennai and Singapore. Over the next minutes:

20:12  mumbai  rps 0        chennai rps 40k -> 95k   singapore rps 30k -> 70k
20:13  chennai hit_ratio 0.95 -> 0.62    origin_rps 12k -> 118k
20:14  origin 5xx 0.2% -> 9%    chennai p99 ttfb 60ms -> 1,400ms

Chennai CPU is at 88%. Origin is a single region.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening, what do you do right now, and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Chennai is overloaded, add servers" with no mention of the cold cache, origin protection or the shield.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Mumbai's cache gone for good or just unreachable? Which objects missed (hot set or long tail)? Is the shield enabled and collapsing? What is the origin's real headroom?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Protect the origin first: serve stale (stale-if-error, stale-while-revalidate) and extend TTLs temporarily. Rate-limit origin fetches per PoP. If possible, shed traffic to a third PoP or a second CDN by weighted DNS.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Chennai and Singapore have caches for their own audience, not Mumbai's; the Mumbai users bring a different hot set, so misses spike. (b) Without a shield or collapsing, many PoPs call the origin directly. (c) Chennai simply lacks CPU/NIC headroom. (d) A red herring: the origin 5xx may be a downstream database, not the CDN.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-PoP hit ratio and miss reason, origin request rate by PoP, shield hit ratio, request-collapse counters, origin DB metrics.
  5. Root cause: Failover moved load onto cold caches, and the miss storm hit a single origin.
  6. Fix: Short-term: serve stale, scale the origin, push the hot set from the shield. Long-term: a regional cache and origin shield so only one request reaches the origin per object, capacity planning at N+1 per region, and anycast with load-aware shedding, and a pre-warm step for failover.
  7. Prevention: Game days that kill a PoP. Alert on origin rps per PoP and a hit-ratio drop.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not simply restore Mumbai's route while its cache is empty. A cold PoP coming back is another miss storm; bring it back at a low weight.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if long TCP connections reset when anycast shifts? -> Expected for some clients; consistent hashing at the PoP and QUIC connection IDs reduce it. Retry logic on the client.
  • What if the origin is down as well? -> Stale-if-error and cached error pages for a few seconds only; never cache 5xx for long.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A PoP failure caused a short brownout not from lost capacity but from cache warmup. The fix was a shield with collapsing, not more edge servers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds servers only.
  • Hire: Identifies cold cache and origin protection, serves stale.
  • Strong hire: Adds shield tier, staged restore, game days and metrics per PoP.

questions.contextHtml: You are choosing how users reach edges: DNS steering (authoritative DNS picks a PoP from the resolver IP or EDNS Client Subnet, TTL 30 s) or anycast (one IP announced from every PoP via BGP). Telemetry shows 18% of your Indian users resolve through a public resolver abroad. A past attack of 600 Gbps saturated one PoP. Some customers have long-lived WebSocket and large downloads.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and how do you justify the decision gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Anycast is faster" or "DNS is simpler", with no discussion of failure handling, DDoS, or the mis-location problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we need load-aware control (shift 20% to another PoP)? Do customers use long-lived TCP? Do we run our own network and BGP, or sit in other people's data centres? What failure detection time do we need?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (design). I would offer a staged approach.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: DNS steering gives fine control (latency, load, health) but reacts at TTL speed and mis-locates users on far resolvers (ECS helps). Anycast fails over automatically via BGP withdrawal and spreads DDoS across all PoPs, but BGP "nearest" is not always lowest latency, it offers little load control and long connections can break when routes change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure real user latency to the anycast-chosen PoP versus the best PoP (RUM beacons), share of ECS-capable resolvers, connection break rate during route changes.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The deciding factors are DDoS resilience and failover speed versus control.
  6. Fix: Use both: anycast for the DNS servers and the entry IPs (resilience, DDoS), DNS-based steering on top for load and cost control (for example shift traffic away from an overloaded PoP), health checks wired to both. Mitigate broken connections with consistent hashing inside a PoP and QUIC connection IDs.
  7. Prevention: RUM latency by PoP, route-change alerts, regular PoP drain drills.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Changing the routing layer is operationally risky but can be done in stages, so it is closer to a reversible decision. What is nearly one-way is the commitment to run BGP and own address space. I would not rely on a short DNS TTL alone for failover; resolvers sometimes ignore it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if one PoP is under DDoS? -> With anycast, attack traffic spreads by origin geography; add scrubbing and rate limits and withdraw that PoP if needed.
  • What about a startup without its own ASN? -> Use DNS steering or buy a provider that already does it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team moved to anycast and saw random download failures. Mid-flow routing shifts reset long TCP connections; range-resume on the client plus QUIC fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks one without trade-offs.
  • Hire: Names failover, DDoS, control, mis-location.
  • Strong hire: Hybrid plan, measures with RUM, handles long connections.

questions.contextHtml:
For 35 minutes yesterday, about 1,200 users of a banking-style dashboard saw another user's account summary. A rule added for performance cached /dashboard for 5 minutes. A log excerpt:

GET /dashboard  cookie: session=abc   200  x-cache: MISS  cache-control: public, max-age=300
GET /dashboard  cookie: session=xyz   200  x-cache: HIT   age: 143

The origin had recently been upgraded; its default response header changed from private to public.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: cause, contributing factors, and the controls you add.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Someone mis-set a header", with no systemic fix, no mention of the cache key or defence in depth.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which paths carried the header? Was the key missing the session? Did the CDN rule override the origin header? How many users were affected and for how long (for disclosure)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Purge the affected path by key, disable caching for authenticated paths at the edge, and ship Cache-Control: private, no-store from the origin. Preserve logs for legal and security teams.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Contributing: origin default flipped to public; CDN rule trusted origin headers; the cache key excluded the cookie; no test for cacheability of authenticated routes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay requests with two sessions against staging; check Vary, Cache-Control, edge rule config history, and the cache key definition.
  5. Root cause: A per-user response was stored under a shared key because it was marked public with no Vary or session in the key.
  6. Fix: Edge default: do not cache requests with Authorization or session cookies unless a path is explicitly allow-listed. Origin: private/no-store by default for authenticated responses. For legitimate personalised caching, include the user in the key or use edge compute to merge a cached shell with per-user JSON.
  7. Prevention: A contract test that fetches a private route with two accounts and asserts different bodies and no shared caching; config changes to cache rules require security review; alert if an authenticated route returns X-Cache: HIT.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not "fix" it by shortening the TTL. Any window can leak. I would not blame the engineer; the system allowed a single header to cause a leak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about signed URLs for private files? -> Separate expiring tokens; ensure the token is not part of the shared key in a way that exposes it, and keep TTL below the token life.
  • Is Vary: Cookie a fix? -> It prevents sharing but destroys hit ratio for public pages; use targeted rules instead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A framework upgrade changed a response default and a CDN rule honoured it. The review's main change was not a header but a default-deny edge policy for authenticated traffic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames one person or one header.
  • Hire: Names cache key, header, CDN rule and fixes them.
  • Strong hire: Default-deny policy, automated two-user test, alerting and disclosure steps.
